transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess... what brings me in is that I just can’t keep my words in a straight line anymore. It’s like, I work as a psych aide, an orderly, right? And I do these really long overnight shifts. They're twelve hours, and you're constantly on your feet, walking the halls, checking the rooms, making sure everything is quiet and everyone is safe. And I’ll try to tell someone about it, just trying to have a normal conversation about how the overnight shift went, and I start talking about the shift, but then somehow I end up jumping to soccer. 

And then from soccer, I'm suddenly talking about paint colors, like the specific shade of beige on the ward walls, and then I'm jumping over to patient charts. And I don't even realize I'm doing it until... well, I can see everyone getting lost. I look at my coworkers or my supervisor, and they just have this confused look, like they have no idea how I got from point A to point B. And I just keep talking, trying to explain it, but it just gets more tangled up. It's really starting to mess up my job because you have to be so clear when you're passing on information about the patients, you know? You can't just be throwing random things into the shift report. But my brain just won't let me talk straight, it just keeps pulling me in all these different directions at once.
During the times when your speech becomes difficult to keep organized, do you need much less sleep than usual without feeling tired?

No, no, not at all. It’s... it's actually kind of the opposite, honestly. I mean, with those overnight shifts—twelve hours of just constant pacing, checking the doors, doing the 15-minute checks on the rooms—I get so unbelievably tired. Like, bone-tired, where your feet are just throbbing by the time you clock out. 

When I get home at like 8:00 AM, the sun is already up, and I have these blackout curtains I bought, the really heavy velvet ones, because you really need it pitch black to trick your brain into thinking it's night. But even with those, I'm just... I'm exhausted. I definitely don't have that thing where I don't need sleep or feel energized. If anything, I want to sleep way more than I even have time for. My body just feels like it weighs a thousand pounds. I'll crash for like nine or ten hours if I can, though usually the garbage trucks or people outside wake me up around two in the afternoon and then I'm just dragging for the rest of the day. 

But yeah, I never have that feeling of being totally fine after just a couple of hours of sleep. Even when my brain is doing that weird jumping around thing with my words and I can't talk straight, I'm still just so, so drained. It's like my mouth is running a marathon but my body is just completely dead weight, you know? So, yeah, no, I definitely still need my sleep. Probably more than a normal person, really, just to survive those shifts.
How long has this difficulty keeping your speech organized been happening?

Well, if I really sit down and trace it back... I'd say it's been going on for about a year and a month now. Yeah, thirteen months. I remember specifically because it was right after I hit my one-year anniversary working at the facility. I was really proud of making it a whole year doing those grueling overnights, you know? It's a tough job and a lot of people quit after a couple of months. But then, almost exactly a month after that work milestone, my brain just started doing this... this slipping thing. 

And honestly, it hasn't just been the talking that's messed up. The disorganized speech, where I jump from one thing to another, that definitely started a year and a month ago, but my actual behavior got all disorganized right at the exact same time too. Like, I'd go into the supply closet to grab fresh linens for a new admission, right? Just a simple, everyday task. But I'd end up standing in there for twenty minutes just rearranging the little soap packets or staring at the mop buckets, completely forgetting what I was even supposed to be doing in the first place. My supervisor actually had to come find me a few times because I'd just wander off track and start doing things that made absolutely no sense for the shift. 

And... well, that was also the exact same time I started getting these really intense beliefs that I was being watched. It's so strong. Especially on the night shift when the halls are supposed to be dead quiet and the lights are dimmed. I'll be walking down the corridor with my clipboard, and I can just feel these eyes burning into the back of my neck, like someone is monitoring every single move I make, scrutinizing me, even when I know for a fact all the patients are in their rooms and the doors are secure. I'll spin around and no one is there, but the feeling doesn't go away. So, yeah, the tangled up words, the messy behavior where I can't finish a task, the constant feeling of being watched by someone... all of that has been happening together for about a year and one month now. It just hasn't let up at all since it started.
Before these symptoms began, were you using or withdrawing from any drugs, alcohol, or prescription medications?

No, no drugs or anything like that. I mean, I don't really even drink. Maybe a beer on my birthday, but that's about it. Working as a psych aide, you see a lot of people come in who are really struggling with substances, detoxing, and it's... it's rough. You see them shaking, sweating through their scrubs, screaming at things that aren't there because the withdrawals are so bad. I've had to hold down guys my own age, guys who are 22 just like me, while the nurses give them something to calm them down because they're coming off meth or heroin or whatever else they got their hands on. 

So, seeing that day in and day out, especially on the night shift when things get really unpredictable, it just completely turned me off to ever messing with any of that stuff. I've never touched illegal drugs in my life, not even weed. And as for prescription meds, I wasn't taking anything back then. I mean, occasionally I'd take an ibuprofen if my back was killing me from lifting patients or moving the heavy beds around, because those beds are surprisingly heavy when the wheels lock up, but that was it. 

I wasn't on any daily medications, no antidepressants, no sleep aids, nothing like that. I was completely clean, totally sober, just drinking way too much coffee from the breakroom machine to stay awake. That coffee is terrible, by the way, it tastes like burnt dirt, but you drink it anyway because you have to keep moving. But yeah, no substances, no withdrawals, nothing chemically that could have triggered all this slipping in my brain or the feeling of being watched. It just... it just started happening on its own, completely out of the blue.
Have you heard voices speaking when no one else was present?

No, no, I haven't heard any voices. I know that's a big thing you guys ask about. I mean, working at the facility, I see it all the time. Patients will be sitting alone in the day room, just staring at the wall, and suddenly they're having a full-blown argument with someone who isn't there. They'll be yelling, gesturing, sometimes even throwing things because whatever the voice is saying is just so real to them, so upsetting. I've had to help de-escalate so many situations where a patient is just terrified of what they're hearing. It's really sad, honestly, to see someone so tormented by something that no one else can hear. 

But for me? No, nothing like that. It's just the feeling of being watched, that heavy, prickling sensation on the back of my neck, like eyes are just drilling into me. And the weird thing with my words getting all jumbled up, and my thoughts slipping around so I can't finish a simple task like grabbing linens. But my ears? My ears are fine. It's perfectly quiet when it's supposed to be quiet. Well, as quiet as it gets on the unit with the hum of the fluorescent lights and the HVAC system constantly kicking on and off. But yeah, no voices, no whispering, no one talking to me when I'm alone. Just... just my own messy brain and that constant, awful feeling that someone is staring right at me.

final_diagnosis.reason: Persistent persecutory delusions, disorganized speech, and grossly disorganized behavior have been present continuously for approximately 13 months, with clear occupational impairment and no reported substance or medication cause. The duration and symptom pattern support schizophrenia over schizophreniform, brief psychotic, or delusional disorder.

confirmed_symptoms: Persistent belief or strong feeling that someone is watching and monitoring the patient despite no one being present
Disorganized speech with frequent derailment and jumping between unrelated topics
Disorganized behavior, including losing track of simple tasks, wandering off task, and rearranging objects instead of completing assigned duties

diagnostic_checklist.duration_verified: Disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, and persecutory beliefs have been present continuously for approximately 13 months.
additional_requirements: Occupational functioning is impaired, including difficulty providing coherent shift reports and requiring supervisor intervention.
No substance use, withdrawal, or medication exposure preceding symptom onset was reported.
No manic pattern was supported; the patient reported marked fatigue and a normal or increased need for sleep rather than decreased need for sleep.
